t: The numbers are heavily contested: chroniclers give figures as high as 400,000 for the combatants, while 19th-century German historians estimated about 7,500 to 15,000 Christians and about 12,000 to 20,000 Turks.
The crusaders had no single commander. Sigismund's advice to let the Turkish vanguard be met by Wallachian foot soldiers was rejected by the French, who insisted on leading the charge.
After the defeat, Western Europe made no further move to stop the Turkish advance in the Balkans until the 1440s, and Constantinople fell in 1453.
dyk: The nearest thing to an eyewitness account was written by Johann Schiltberger, who was 16 when he saw the battle, was captured and spent 30 years enslaved by the Turks before he returned home and wrote it.
ev: After the Battle of Kosovo the Ottomans conquer most of the Balkans
Pope Boniface IX proclaims a new crusade against the Turks, and the Ottomans begin to blockade Constantinople
The crusade sets out from Dijon for Buda
The crusaders come within view of Nicopolis and begin the siege
The French charge, are met by Bayezid's reserve of sipahis, and the crusader army is routed
Bayezid has the prisoners brought before him, and many are executed while the nobles are spared for ransom
A ransom of 200,000 gold florins is agreed, and the noble prisoners are released on 24 June
Hungarians, Poles and Wallachians are defeated at the Battle of Varna

f.place: Before the fortress of Nicopolis on the lower Danube
f.sides: A crusader army under King Sigismund of Hungary, with a French contingent nominally led by John, Count of Nevers, against an Ottoman force under Sultan Bayezid I. Numbers are heavily contested: 19th-century German historians reached about 7,500 to 15,000 Christians and about 12,000 to 20,000 Turks, while chroniclers give far higher figures.
f.outcome: The crusaders were routed. Many were killed or captured, Sigismund escaped by boat, and the siege of Nicopolis was lifted.
